content: The Rockefeller drug laws refer to a set of statutes in the New York State Penal Law that govern the sale and possession of narcotic drugs. These laws were named after Nelson Rockefeller, who was the governor of New York at the time of their enactment. Governor Rockefeller, a strong proponent of these laws, signed the legislation on May 8, 1973. Under these laws, the penalties for selling two ounces (approximately 56 grams) or more of substances such as heroin, morphine, raw or prepared opium, cocaine, or cannabis—including marijuana—were made equivalent to the penalties for second-degree murder. Specifically, individuals convicted of these offenses faced a minimum sentence of 15 years to life in prison and a maximum sentence of 25 years to life. It is important to note that while cannabis and marijuana were included in the statute, they are not chemically classified as narcotics. The original version of the legislation also proposed the same severe penalties for committing violent crimes while under the influence of these drugs. However, this provision was ultimately removed before the bill was signed into law. In 1979, the section of the Rockefeller drug laws that applied to marijuana was repealed under the administration of Democratic Governor Hugh Carey. The Rockefeller drug laws were considered the harshest drug-related statutes in the United States at the time of their adoption. This approach was later emulated by Michigan in 1978 with the enactment of the 650-Lifer Law. Michigan's law mandated life imprisonment without the possibility of parole for individuals convicted of selling, manufacturing, or possessing at least 650 grams (approximately 1.45 pounds) of cocaine or any Schedule I or Schedule II opiate. Both the New York and Michigan laws faced significant criticism from across the political spectrum. Conservative figures, such as William F. Buckley, and many members of law enforcement opposed these laws, arguing that equating non-violent drug offenses with murder was inherently unjust. Civil rights advocates also condemned the laws, asserting that they were disproportionately applied to African Americans and, to a lesser extent, Latinos, thereby perpetuating racial inequities. Michigan's statute underwent reform in 1998, reducing the mandatory life sentence to a minimum of 20 years. In New York, significant reforms were introduced on December 14, 2004, when Governor George Pataki signed the Drug Law Reform Act (DLRA) into law. This legislation, which took effect on January 13, 2005, replaced the indeterminate sentencing structure of the Rockefeller drug laws with a determinate sentencing system. It also reduced mandatory minimum prison sentences for non-violent felony drug offenders. For the most serious drug offense (classified as an A-I felony), the minimum penalty for first-time offenders was reduced from 15 years to life to 8 years in prison. Additionally, the weight thresholds for the two most severe possession offenses (A-I and A-II felonies) were doubled. The DLRA also allowed individuals serving life sentences under the Rockefeller drug laws to apply for re-sentencing. Since the implementation of these reforms in 2004, the number of individuals incarcerated for A-I narcotics felonies in New York has decreased by more than half.
